ancestry_summary.statement_nl: Let a, b, r be integers with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0. Set I := {a+1, a+2, ..., b}, and let R := Q[x_s : s in I] be the polynomial ring graded by deg(x_s) = s for each s in I. For each positive integer d define M_d(u,v) := |{m in Z : u < m <= v and d divides m}|. Assume M_d(r+a, r+b) >= M_d(a,b) for every positive integer d. Then there exists a family (f_s)_{s in I} of homogeneous polynomials in R such that deg(f_s) = r+s for every s in I, and the ordered list of these polynomials in increasing order of s is a regular sequence in R. If I is empty, this means the empty family.

ancestry_summary.statement_nl: Let a, b, r, j be integers with 0 <= a <= b, r >= 0, and 0 <= j <= floor(r (b - a) / 2). Put I := {a+1, a+2, ..., b}. For each positive integer d, define M_d(u,v) := |{m in Z : u < m <= v and d divides m}|, and assume M_d(r+a,r+b) >= M_d(a,b) for every positive integer d. Let X_j be the set of pairs (S, lambda) such that S is a subset of I, lambda is a finite multiset of elements of I, |lambda| denotes the sum of the elements of lambda, and |lambda| + sum_{s in S} (r + s) = j. Then there exists an involution iota_j : X_j -> X_j such that: (1) if iota_j(S,lambda) = (S',lambda') != (S,lambda), then |S'| is congruent to |S| + 1 modulo 2; and (2) if iota_j(S,lambda) = (S,lambda), then |S| is even.

ancestry_summary.statement_nl: Let [n choose k]_q denote the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient. Prove that for all integers n, k, ℓ with 0 ≤ k, ℓ ≤ n, if [n choose k]_q / [n choose ℓ]_q is a polynomial in q, then it has only nonnegative coefficients.

payload.proof_nl:
Fix an arbitrary positive integer d. Define
A := {i in {1,...,b} : d divides e_i}
and
B := {i in {1,...,b} : d divides i}.

We split the index set {1,...,b} into the disjoint union {1,...,a} union {a+1,...,b}. (If a=0 or a=b, one of these sets is empty, and the same argument still applies.) Therefore A is the disjoint union of A ∩ {1,...,a} and A ∩ {a+1,...,b}, and similarly for B.

For i with 1 <= i <= a, the definition gives e_i = i. Hence
|A ∩ {1,...,a}| = |{i in {1,...,a} : d divides i}|.

For i with a < i <= b, the definition gives e_i = r+i. The map i -> r+i is a bijection from {a+1,...,b} onto the set {m in Z : r+a < m <= r+b}. Under this bijection, the condition d divides e_i is exactly the condition d divides m. Thus
|A ∩ {a+1,...,b}| = |{m in Z : r+a < m <= r+b and d divides m}| = M_d(r+a,r+b).

Since the two pieces are disjoint,
|A| = |{i in {1,...,a} : d divides i}| + M_d(r+a,r+b).

Now do the same for B. Clearly,
|B ∩ {1,...,a}| = |{i in {1,...,a} : d divides i}|.
Also, the identity map is a bijection from {a+1,...,b} onto {m in Z : a < m <= b}, so
|B ∩ {a+1,...,b}| = |{m in Z : a < m <= b and d divides m}| = M_d(a,b).
Therefore,
|B| = |{i in {1,...,a} : d divides i}| + M_d(a,b).

By the hypothesis of the lemma, for this positive integer d we have
M_d(r+a,r+b) >= M_d(a,b).
Comparing the formulas for |A| and |B|, we obtain
|A| >= |B|,
that is,
|{i in {1,...,b} : d divides e_i}| >= |{i in {1,...,b} : d divides i}|.

Because d was arbitrary, this holds for every positive integer d, exactly as claimed.

payload.statement_nl: Let a, b, r be integers with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0. For 1 <= i <= b define an integer e_i by e_i = i when i <= a, and e_i = r+i when a < i <= b. For each positive integer d define M_d(u,v) := |{m in Z : u < m <= v and d divides m}|. If M_d(r+a, r+b) >= M_d(a,b) for every positive integer d, then for every positive integer d one has |{i in {1,...,b} : d divides e_i}| >= |{i in {1,...,b} : d divides i}|.

detailed_findings.finding: Correctly fixes an arbitrary positive integer d and proves the target inequality for that d, then quantifies over all positive integers d at the end.
The split of {1,...,b} into {1,...,a} and {a+1,...,b} is used appropriately, including the edge cases where one part is empty.
The bijection i -> r+i from {a+1,...,b} to the interval of integers r+a < m <= r+b is exactly the right translation to convert the count into M_d(r+a,r+b).

result_payload.reason: The proof is a complete direct counting argument. For fixed positive d, it partitions the index set {1,...,b} into {1,...,a} and {a+1,...,b}, uses the definition e_i=i on the first part and e_i=r+i on the second, and identifies the second-part count with M_d(r+a,r+b). Doing the same for divisibility of i identifies the comparison count with M_d(a,b). The assumed inequality then gives the desired result. The proof matches the lemma statement and assembly role, and it uses no undeclared or forbidden dependencies.
